The most notable instance of this occurred within the Learn section where students were supposed to self-select strategies to solve 12x8. The teacher consulted the visuals provided on the first TE page for this activity and modeled these for students, rather than releasing responsibility. Throughout this activity and other points in the lesson, the teacher had their back to students, with their head down (consulting the TE). Additionally, the pacing of the lesson was only partially aligned in Fluency/Launch and Learn, whereas Land did not occur within the lesson time frame. Fluency was 11 minutes over the provided 10-minute time stamp, and Learn was facilitated within 35 minutes (and was not fully completed, as students were not finished with the assigned Problem Set problems before they had to move on for the day).",1,"The teacher facilitated the lesson without using curriculum-embedded activities and questions when appropriate. L23 calls for think-pair-shares throughout each segment to provide students opportunities to observe and discuss patterns within multiples of 11 and 12. Students also are given the opportunity to self-select a strategy to solve 12x8 and visually display this strategy (in collaboration with a partner). The teacher facilitated whole group discussion for each discourse opportunity listed in the TE, often asking yes/no questions or for a specific number as an answer to fill in the blank. Instead of allowing students to choose a strategy, the teacher modeled three strategies they chose from the TE, and the students copied them down. This impacted student engagement and proficiency with L23's Key Questions and purpose.",1,"The teacher released responsibility to students less than 50% of the time, and less than 50% of tasks maintained their rigor. The only two tasks that were facilitated nearly as written were the Fluency activity, in which the teacher released responsibility to students throughout and challenged them with reframing their answers (as indicated in the TE and support notes), and the Problem Set, which was facilitated as an independent opportunity for students to solve problems related to the lesson's concept. Every other activity (of which there were 3 more) was simplified or facilitated with the teacher completing the work and thinking for the students. This resulted in a low cognitive lift for students throughout the lesson, although engagement and excitement peaked for students during the 40% of the time they received responsibility.",2,"The teacher provided one opportunity for student-to-student discourse that resulted in a more precise answer aligned to the goals of L23. During the Counting Twelves activity, the teacher provided a turn-and-talk moment for students with the question: ""What patterns are we noticing with our 12’s?"" While this was not a curriculum-embedded question, this question allowed students to observe the patterns after the graphic organizer had been filled out. Students articulated the differences in the 10's and 1's place between each row, consolidating the pattern that can be observed until 12x5 for the class. The two student volunteers that articulated the pattern details used appropriate and precise math language to accurately describe an intended lesson goal.",1,"The teacher did not administer any curriculum-embedded assessment. For L23, this would have been an Exit Ticket. ",1,"The teacher did not provide feedback on student work during the observation. Student work was observed for compliance with directions, and any circulation by the teacher was either for compliance or to verify if students had followed what had been written down on the board. This resulted in student dependency on the teacher for directions, guidance, and verification frequently during the lesson time. The teacher extended the 10-minute Fluency timing by 6 minutes to complete every activity and every problem. This set up students for success but shortened the time needed for key lesson components. The teacher also had to stop the lesson right before the Which One Doesn't Belong? routine at the 34-minute mark of Learn. The Land did not occur. Students were not able to reflect on their learning as a result.",2,"The teacher facilitated curriculum-specific elements with some alignment to their purpose. L15 emphasizes a progression within the main activity of Learn (Estimate and Measure Time) that allows students to use benchmarks to make informed estimates. This language and logic were omitted. L15 also calls for students making an estimate and decision on units of time (seconds vs. minutes), completing an activity, and then repeating this process to complete the provided graphic organizer. When the teacher had students complete all estimates before doing any activities, this further deviated from allowing benchmarks to guide estimates for students. This affected students' ability to estimate primarily, but it also affected students' ability to generalize that the smaller the unit, the more units it takes to measure. This was also reflected in the omission of a turn-and-talk opportunity (""Invite students to think–pair–share about why each activity took more seconds than minutes."").",2,"The teacher maintains the rigor of tasks between 50%–75% of the time. L15 calls for students to record the actual time it takes to complete the listed activities in the graphic organizer. Instead of recording the actual time, the teacher had students round their answers to the nearest whole number (even if it was down). This modification reduced the rigor of the lesson and reduced the cognitive load for students, because not only did it prevent students from reading the analog clock to accurately record the actual time, but the rounding was facilitated entirely by the teacher with no student input. This was one of three major opportunities for cognitive lift in the lesson, reducing the lift by 33%. ",1,"The teacher throughout the lesson did not facilitate student-to-student discourse when it was called for in the TE. Every instance of think-pair-share was omitted by the teacher. L8 has a 35-minute time allotment for Learn, and this is composed of 3 distinct sections of instructional before the Problem Set. The teacher facilitated Learn as one, single problem from the Learn section (Make Equivalent Fraction, problem #3) before moving on to the Problem Set. This took 30 minutes of instructional time during the observation. Additionally, the Launch and Land were not facilitated in alignment with their suggested pacing. Launch was facilitated in 3 minutes, and the Land was facilitated in 4 minutes.",1,"The teacher skipped pedagogical elements and facilitated the lesson without using the curriculum-embedded questions when appropriate. L8 features a Math Chat in the Launch. This was omitted from the lesson, with the teacher facilitating a procedural solving method for producing an equivalent fraction. This limited the conceptual understanding of equivalent fractions and their visual representations for students, impacting their ability to effectively compare, order, and combine fractions in the future. Additionally, the lines of questioning that are included for L8's TE were omitted, preventing student-to-student collaboration and exploration.",1,"The teacher released responsibility to students less than 50% of the time. The rigor of tasks was maintained less than 50% of the time. Student responsibility was only released for the completed Fluency activity (comparing fractions) and the Exit Ticket. It was initially released for the Problem Set. The teacher eventually began completing problems on the board during the Problem Set work time, essentially doing the work for the students and allowing anyone in the classroom to copy down the answers without conceptual or procedural understanding. With the omission of the majority of the learning activities in L8, the teacher greatly reduced the rigor of the lesson in favor of facilitating one method for producing an equivalent fraction. With the Exit Ticket, during the provided work time, students were getting up from their desks to both turn in the Exit Ticket (for those that understood the concept) and consult with peers. Several students had a peer complete the work for them and/or consulted with a peer (looking at their answers and copying, getting verification if they were correct, etc.), thus lowering the rigor of this task.",1,"The teacher provided two opportunities for student-to-student discourse during the lesson. Neither of these opportunities promoted deeper or more precise thinking, and neither of them were opportunities outlined in the TE for L8. One of these opportunities was during the Fluency section of the lesson, where the teacher had students turn-and-talk about problem #2, which was comparing 1/3 vs. 1/3. All students in the class turned to compare their answers, but little to no discourse occurred to promote deeper or more precise answers (as this question was one of the simpler ones for students to compare). During the Land facilitation, the teacher asked students to turn-and-talk about how the class could get different answers for the Exit Ticket and still be correct. However, no one spoke to a partner, and the majority of the class (except for 6 students) was not involved or listening to this Land discussion.",1,"The teacher did administer a curriculum-embedded assessment (L8's Exit Ticket), but the teacher did not circulate throughout the lesson time. There is one instance of teacher circulation noted, and that was to redirect a group that was off-task and had not been on-task up until that point. There were no checks for understanding, no monitoring of student work, etc. Additionally, while the Exit Ticket was administered, students did not complete the Exit Ticket independently. Answers to the Exit Ticket were also shown to students in the middle of their work time to promote the Land discussion. Not all students had finished and handed in their assessment before the teacher facilitated an examination of student work, and this resulted in many students copying answers or having their peers complete their work for them.",1,"The teacher did not provide feedback on student work but did provide feedback on students’ adherence to directions. L8 features many opportunities for students to practice the lesson's skills and strategies. It also features the opportunity for students to vocalize patterns and noticings. The teacher, in facilitating this lesson without those elements, limited the opportunities for feedback. Additionally, without circulation to monitor student work, the teacher was unable to provide actionable feedback to students based on their performance.",1,"Less than 75% of students were engaged and on task during collaborative activities.
